sentences.text: No, our office is in Windsor.
This meeting is being recorded.
I live sort of north west of London.
How about you?
I used to live in northwest London.
Okay, fair enough.
I'm out in Somerset now.
Okay, cool.
We're near a town called Bruton which is like a nice arty place.
Oh, amazing.
Sounds good.
Bad.
About an hour, hour and 10 minutes on the train to into London as well.
So all pretty cozy and good.
Well, nice to meet you and thanks for your time today you submitted a form on Agencies Co.
So yeah, I'm, I'm just really trying to explore some options at the moment and, and just trying to understand a bit more about what I can get out of the platform.
Yeah, I can give you a quick rundown of, you know, who we are and where we are.
Yeah, that would be great.

Well, why don't I, I start, I'll talk to you to talk you through who we are and what we do and then it be great to get into what it is that you're trying to achieve and what you do at your agency and then I can go through a few options with you.
That's good, that sounds good.
So we are capital A, we're an M and A advisory and we only work in marketing services.
So we either work on the buy or the sell side.

On the buy side we work with either private equity or fast high growth agencies that are looking to grow through acquisitions and agencies CO is our sell side marketplace for buyers and sellers of agencies.
And yeah, we.
Let me have a look.
We.
In the last, I would say 12 months we've worked on transactions, roughly about $100 million of transactions on, on both buy and sell side.

So we're fairly active and obviously because we make offers on a lot of agencies as well for our buy side clients, we've got a really good feel for the market and what our agency sell side clients are worth as well.

So it'd be good to understand a little bit more about Pixel Eggs be if, I mean if you could talk me through a little bit about what it is that you do, how long you've been going, who's on your team, where your revenue and EBITDA is and what you're looking to achieve.
Yeah, I can, I can explain all that.
So I, I started the company coming up to 14 years ago.
Now my background is in, in technology and development.
I've always worked agency side though, so I used to work at a couple of sort of large London agencies in the past and we've grown quite organically.
I would Say over there over that time.
We're now 19 people and I've got everyone that I need to do the work that we do all in house.
So it's, we're really more a design and development agency.
We're design and build rather than marketing if you like.
And is that all websites or is it apps?
It is all.
Well, we used to do apps.
To be honest, no one's asked us for one for about, I don't know, maybe four years now.
Okay, don't do apps anymore then.
I just don't.
Yeah, I just don't think it's that much of a thing anymore.
So most of what we do is build people's company websites that they keep for, you know, five, six, seven, sometimes longer years.
So it's not so much on the sort of fast moving microsite type things.
It's more that the sort of that site that people keep for a while.
We work a lot with the charity sector and with sort of also with for profits but that sort of sit within either education or some kind of environmental organization.
We're B Corp.
So you know, our sector if you like is sort of purpose driven organizations.
That's who we work with.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And we're getting more and more into sort of content services as things change and sort of AI sort of starts to have a bit of an impact on what we're doing.
But our core capabilities are around UX design and development.
Okay.
In terms of team, I've got, I mean I mentioned I've got everyone that I need.
I've actually got quite a good senior experienced team of people.
I've got a really senior team of developers, most of whom I've been working with for, you know, some of them over 20 years.
And my design team also made up of someone I used to work with many years ago that you know, who came into the agency quite early on and helped establish a design offering.

We started off as a development only agency but we, you know, we have lots of really capable people within the team and I've got a good sort of senior management team as well now across project management, design development and client services.
And that's kind of how we're set up to work in the sort of the 10 years, I guess or nine years before COVID We were always profitable.
We were actually doing quite well.
There was a.
We were about two weeks away when Covid hit from signing on a much bigger office in London.
It still ended up costing us a little bit of money while we pulled out of it because it just sort of didn't seem like it was going to be something that was going to go away anytime soon.
However, since COVID I think, you know, the sector we work with has been impacted.
So, you know, we, we had a lot of charity clients there, budgets were cut.
That impact impacted us immediately.
And even though it's kind of recovered a little bit, it's, you know, the last five years were very different to the previous nine to that.
So we, we've survived, we've done okay, but it's nowhere near sort of as profitable as it was before, which is why I'm not really sure whether the timing of all this is right or not.
But I still wanted to sort of think about what I do and, and have a bit of a conversation about it because, yeah, I'm sort of at that stage where I'm wondering what, what my next move should be.
Whether it's a, an expansion drive or, or whether it is to sort of sell and, and think about something else.
Yeah.
And what, what's your revenue change look like over the past five years versus the previous nine?
Is it, is it vastly different?
So, I mean, we, I think our revenue has actually increased a little bit over the last five years.
So we, last year we were just under one and a half million pounds.
But it's the profit, profitability.
So your profitability gone up.
You know, you, you found it more difficult to get stuff done as everything expensive.
Yeah.
And also I think the budgets have dropped a little bit over the last few years.
So, you know, we're now working with budgets that we're seeing in 2014 as opposed to what we're seeing in sort of 2019.
So you've got more clients, so you are winning more business, but they're just spending less.
We are, we're winning.
I mean, we're okay at winning business.
We sort of, we tend to win, especially if we set our minds to it.
We do actually tend to win more than we lose.
And at least half of our income now comes from retained clients as well.
So we're a lot less reliant on project work than we were before.
The thing that happened during the COVID time is that we became a little bit less efficient.
I think is the honest truth of it is, you know, while we were trying to learn how to work remotely, we weren't as efficient as when we were all into.
In a room together and we had to go and invest in more people to sort of service the work that we had because we were a little bit less efficient and we never fully recovered from that.
So I think this year was a little bit different.
But even then it's been kind of difficult and I've got a.
What I think is a relatively lean team now.
So, you know, 19 people were all doers, effectively is, you know, it's, it's more people than we had before to service the same sort of amount of money.
If you like revenue, okay, that's, that's.
Understandable, but interesting, really interesting.
Okay, so.
So if you had your way, then, when would you want to be out the business?
What, what's kind of going on personally?
I mean, the personal stuff is, it's, you know, my kids have now left home and everything else.
You don't look old enough.
I definitely am.
So I'm, I'm.
Yeah, I'm.
I guess I'm sort of planning in the next sort of two, three years to see if I can step away from things, and that could take a few different ways to do things, I guess.
I have looked at an employee ownership trust.
I'm not entirely sure it's the right thing to do at the moment, but it's interesting.
But I'm kind of interested to see what we might be worth, even though the timing of it might not be great.
So the 110k that you're doing at the moment in profits, is that.
Is that kind of what it looks like now going forward, or have you had, like, particularly expensive years?
Where are you with.
With the profit margins?
So I think that's what this year is going to look like.
I'm doing a little bit of planning for next year.
And yeah, I'm.
To be honest, I'm.
I'm probably in a position where I'm going to have to make some decisions about the team a little bit.
We've got people, for example, in client services that, you know, we can't really not have those people, but we might actually need project managers running client services.
I need to look at our entire makeup a little bit more.
What I do have is a really strong design team and a really strong development team and actually now a really strong project management team.

So we've just hired another senior pm, but I do have like a junior marketing person, so, you know, maybe two or three people where we can sort of cut costs a little bit to try and hit more sort of profitable measures, I guess.
But it's.
I'm not quite there yet.
I just sort of want to see if there's a way.
Yeah.
What's your number?
What would you say is the number that you, that you need or are looking to get to for you to want to exit.
I mean honestly I, I mean I can come up with a number but I, I don't actually know what we would be worth.
I think that's kind of what I'm trying to understand is whether there is a market for an agency like ours because we don't do things like PPC or you know, the SEO stuff we do is all organic.
It's not really paid.
Yeah, well, we've just done a web design company in New York and I mean the interest levels are really high for web design.
So I think, I don't know whether there's been a renaissance or what it is with web design but it's all coming back.
Everybody obviously still needs it.
It's really important to have a good solid website that's well designed with clear ux.
I mean what, what do you think I should look for realistically?
Well, so look smaller agencies, less than 1 million EBITDA.
There's a range 3 to 5x which is kind of standard for, for marketing agencies and these smaller agencies are at the bottom end of that range.
That doesn't mean that you would just get a 3x necessarily.
The fact you're a B corp and you're doing something that is purpose driven.
There's a lot of companies that are still investing in that type of work and it could be that we find the right buyer who's willing to pay a little bit more.
So I would say just from a gut feel, looking at your website, it's a nice looking site, done some nice work with clients.
People have heard of that.
We would probably shoot for around a 4x now, 110k.
That may or may not be enough for you to let go of the reins, but it is.
440000 pounds.
You would get it tax efficiently at least for now I think at 10%.
So it would be a nice way to take some money off the table and then maybe try something else.
It's quite likely as well because of the size and the fact that you've got such a senior team that you might be able to step back very quickly from the business.
So I would suggest unless you have a much bigger number that you need to hit the right time to go to market is when you start thinking about it pretty much.
Because once, once you kind of started thinking about selling, it can almost only get progressively harder to keep maintaining where you are.
Like you're saying you have to cut people.
It's always A roller coaster.
And the emotional part of it, when you're, when you've kind of checked out or you're ready to check out, it just becomes increasingly more difficult.
I've seen so many agencies over the years where they've said they want to sell next year or they want to sell in three years because they're not quite where they want to be.
And I've revisited those agencies in one and three years and it's only got worse because you know, they just want to sell and that, that's the basics of it.
And it's really difficult to double the size of an agency when you've just had enough basically.
So.
Enough?

Yeah, I mean the only thing I've been thinking about is because, you know, like I said, at least half our revenue, so I think it's around about £700,000 actually at the moment, comes from retained clients and 12 month agreements.
I just wonder if there was a bit more value in the business because of that.
Yeah, there definitely is more value in it because of that.
But, but there is this kind of a ceiling for smaller agencies.
That's the only thing.
So.
Okay, it could look, I, I would say go to, to market with a, the strongest story that we can and the best multiple we can get and then let the buyers knock us down a little bit.

But as long as you're realistic then you know, you're happy to walk away at 4x then, then that's cool to do that because there will be that one buyer that just wants the company and they're willing to pay a little bit more.
So it's worth pricing it a little bit extra.
Okay, and how does the process work then?
So do I, do I just have a discussion with you guys?
This, I guess some paperwork gets created and, and then you would list us, is that right?
Yeah, so there's, there's a couple of ways of doing it.

Either you can just list your, yourself and obviously it's fairly cheap then to test the market because once you've, you've got the listing up, it goes out to our mailing list, 20,000 agency owners and buyers and we can get a lot of responses within the first 24 hours.
But obviously you've got a lot of guessing to do on your own.
However, once we do get a buyer on the hook, we help you all the way through that entire process and we're on your side and we'll get the deal done.
And we also take 5% on the deal or 10% of the cash at close and that's netted against the cost of listing which is about £2,000.
But I think the most sensible way to do it is our standard approach which is basically we help you get set up.
So we will do a full valuation of the business.
We'll sort of do a ton of research into the exact work you're doing.
We'll look at similar agencies that have gone to market and sold so we can do some comparables like for, like so we'll give you a price for, for the agency.
We prepare all of the marketing materials for you which includes something called a SIM CIM which is confidential information memorandum which is just like a pitch deck or a brochure.
And we, we do all of the, the listing and the teasers and everything else and then that goes out to our mailing list on Agencies co.
But also we'll build a bespoke list of likely buyers.
So we'll actually research the market and find other buyers that look like they would buy this type of agency.
So we do a lot of work and make sure that we're getting your listing in front of a lot more eyeballs.
So that is slightly more expensive.
It's about four times the price.
It's around £8,000.
But that makes sure kind of that you've got everything right.
You've got your ducks in a row and you get to, not only to market through the platform but also we're obviously doing a proper M A advisory work for you.
So that's probably the most suitable.
And then we do have a slightly more advanced version of that but really it's for larger agencies that are looking to get the business sold within a six month window.
So there's three kind of tiers in terms of our pricing.
I'll send you the link in here and you can have a look at our price.
It's all in dollars because the majority of our clients are US based.
Okay, thank you.
And, and is it, is it like time limited so or you know, let's say I go for a eight grand package and we don't find a buyer in six months time, what happens?
We, we just keep going.
We just keep going.
We don't have a problem with listings staying up.
And obviously sometimes it does take a little bit longer.
I would say kind of nine times out of ten it's quicker and the other nine times out of ten it's longer.
So it's really.
You either hit the six months.
Exactly.
It's pretty precise process.
It takes a couple of months to get momentum going.
It takes A couple of months of talking to buyers and then actually the due diligence process takes 30 to 60 days as well.
So in terms of just getting up and running and the due diligence and contract process anyway, it kind of all ends up being around six months start to finish.
But it does go a little bit quicker for some people and a little bit slower for others, so.
Okay.
All right.
Okay.
I'm going to speak to my accountant and just get some sort of proper figures from him.
Yeah.
And so in terms of the figures, we need the last three years.
The.
P L and the balance sheet and also the current year.
And really during due diligence, when we've got a buyer, they'll want to know what your forecast is as well.
So really it's like five years worth of accounts, the previous three, the current one, and one into the future as well.
And then we'll do a bunch of information requests during onboarding as well.
So we'll do a deep dive.
If you take the standard package, we'll do a deep dive kickoff call.

We'll, we'll get a ton of information from you, but also request stuff like contracts and organograms and all sorts of other stuff that, that just goes into a data room that we start building for you as well.
Okay.
And, and I'm guessing, so you mentioned it's confidential.
I'm guessing there is no chance of my people finding out early that, you know, until there is something done, it's.
A good idea not to tell anybody because it just scares the chickens.
So.
Yeah, no, I don't want to do that.
That's why I'm sort of conscious about it being online in any format.
But it's, it is completely confidential.
So the way that our process works, we've got listings that are, are anonymous listings on the website.
We, we don't use anything from the seller.
We write all of our own listing.
So it does, it's not based on your content.
On your website, for instance, we just write everything fresh so people can't usually Google phrases and, and find where it's coming from.
So yeah, completely anonymous.
Somebody has to sign an NDA on our platform.
Once that NDA is signed, we clear it with you manually.
So it's not like an automated process.
We check that.
You definitely said these guys can get the sim and if you're okay with that, we send them the sim manually as well.
So there's not like a, an opportunity for the system to mess up.
It's all double checked by humans and then once they've got the sim, they've got the name of the business at that point.
Okay.
All right, cool.
Thank you, Andy.
That's really helpful.
Yeah.
I'll have a couple of chats and then maybe I'll come back to you in the next few days.
Okay, brilliant.
All right.
If I don't hear from you in the next couple of days, I'll follow up early next week and see where you heads up.
All right, Sounds good.
Thanks.
All right.
Yeah.
Have a great.
Cheers.
Bye.
Bye.

summary.overview:
- **Business Valuation**: Pixeled Eggs valued at £440,000, based on £1.5 million revenue and 4x EBITDA multiple.
  - Business valuation for Pixeled Eggs is based on a multiple of EBITDA, which reflects the company's profitability and operational efficiency.
  - The estimated valuation of £440,000 is derived from a 4x EBITDA multiple applied to the current profit level of £110,000.
  - This valuation approach is common in the marketing services sector, where agency valuations typically range from 3x to 5x EBITDA based on market demand and growth potential.  
- **Profitability Concerns**: Current profits at £110,000, narrowed by client budget cuts and increased expenses post-COVID.  
- **Sale Process Overview**: Structured sale process costs around £8,000, with options for basic listings at £2,000.  
- **Market Demand**: Strong interest in web design agencies, with recent sales highlighting buyer eagerness for quality websites.  
- **Strategic Planning**: Focus on client retention and operational restructuring to boost margins before a possible sale in 2-3 years.  
- **Confidentiality Emphasis**: Maintaining confidentiality is crucial to protect team morale and client relations during the sale process.
summary.short_summary: The discussion focused on the valuation and sale of Pixeled Eggs, a marketing agency with £1.5 million in revenue and £110,000 in profits. Andy Day assessed the business's value at approximately £440,000 based on a 4x EBITDA multiple, influenced by its B Corp status and purpose-driven client base. Sepas Seraj expressed concerns about profitability and market timing, considering options such as expansion or sale. A structured sale process was outlined, including advisory services for full valuation and buyer outreach, costing around £8,000. Market interest in web design agencies is strong, and there is an emphasis on confidentiality during the sale process. Strategic planning for team restructuring and improved margins before a potential sale in the next 2-3 years was also discussed.
